**Constructed class-practical case.** A teacher-approved fictitious class practical concerns everyday routines that adults use to take breaks while studying. Eight volunteers aged 17 or over consent to individual eight-minute interviews. A student uses the same opening questions for everyone, but may ask neutral follow-up questions. The interviewer is also the participants’ study-group coordinator. Interviews are private; identifying details are removed from the transcripts. No questions concern diagnoses or distressing personal experiences.

Explain two features that make this a semi-structured interview rather than a structured interview.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: An interview obtains an account through interaction between an interviewer and a participant. Here the common opening questions create a consistent starting point, so each participant has an opportunity to discuss the same broad issue of study breaks. This consistency does not make the procedure fully structured.

The permission to ask additional neutral questions makes it semi-structured. For example, an interviewer could ask what a participant means by “a proper break”, then explore that meaning without offering an answer. A structured interview fixes the questions and usually their order, giving less freedom to follow an unanticipated account.

Compare and contrast using these semi-structured interviews with using an anonymous open-ended questionnaire for the same aim.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Both methods can collect participants’ descriptions in their own words, so both can reveal meanings that a fixed-choice habit checklist would miss. Neither automatically establishes what participants actually do during an unobserved study session: each relies on self-report.

The interview permits clarification of an ambiguous phrase such as “often”. This can deepen the account, but the coordinator’s presence can influence what is said. An anonymous questionnaire removes that immediate relationship and may improve candour, while offering no live opportunity to check what a short answer means.

Anonymity also changes the practical options. The questionnaire can be completed independently at a convenient time, but a researcher cannot follow up with a particular respondent after identities have been irreversibly removed. The choice should therefore follow whether depth of meaning or reduced interpersonal pressure is more important to the aim.

title: The staffroom recruitment boundary — Method knowledge
stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** In this fictitious practical, a class interviews adults about convenient ways to build movement breaks into a working day. The researcher approaches the first six consenting staff members present in a school staffroom at lunchtime. The interviews use a fixed question list. Staff who work at other sites or have lunchtime duties cannot be approached there. The questions concern practical preferences, not illness, and participation has no link to employment assessment.

Explain why this is opportunity sampling and distinguish it from random sampling.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: The researcher selects people who are conveniently available in one place at one time. Being a member of staff is not sufficient for selection: a person must also happen to be in this staffroom at lunchtime and agree to take part. Those accessibility conditions make the sample an opportunity sample.

Random sampling instead requires a defined sampling frame and a chance-based selection procedure. Approaching the first six people does not give everyone on the staff list a known selection opportunity, even if the researcher feels that the staffroom contains a varied group. Random selection would also remain distinct from whether selected staff consent.

steps.text: Both approaches select a subset of a wider staff population and both require voluntary, informed consent. Neither can compel a chosen adult to be interviewed. The same fixed interview list could be used with either sample, so differences in sampling need not be confused with differences in interview wording.

A stratified random approach first groups a complete staff list by relevant work role, then makes chance-based selections within those groups. title: An interviewer who shares the routine — Method knowledge
stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** A fictitious class interview explores how adults choose a regular bedtime routine. The student interviewer strongly favours leaving devices outside the bedroom. Four consenting adults aged 18 or over describe their own preferences in private semi-structured interviews. Before analysing the transcripts, the interviewer notices that the follow-up questions were longer when a participant also preferred leaving a device outside. No actual study or clinical assessment is proposed here.

Explain the role of reflexivity in this qualitative research situation.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Reflexivity means examining how the researcher’s position, expectations and choices may influence the research process. In this case it includes recognising that a personal preference about devices shaped which answers received longer follow-up questions. This is more specific than simply saying that the interviewer has an opinion.

A reflexive record could document the preference, identify the points at which questioning became uneven and explain how later interviewing or interpretation was changed. It does not erase the uneven transcripts already produced. Its value is to make the researcher’s contribution visible and open to critical assessment.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Inter-observer reliability concerns consistency between observers applying the coding rules. This concerns agreement about what was recorded, not whether the rule captures the entire construct of participation.

If the aim is broad participation, excluding material arrangement and short gestures may omit important contributions. A measure can therefore be reliable yet incomplete for that aim. It would be more defensible to describe the outcome narrowly as extended spoken turns than as all forms of participation.

stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** A fictitious class survey asks adult members of a community club about preferred ways of organising shared activities. With permission, a researcher obtains a current membership list divided into daytime and evening members. They randomly select invitations within each group. Selected members receive the same short questionnaire, but several say that the phrase “regular contact” is unclear. Participation is voluntary, and membership administrators cannot see individual answers.

Explain how this procedure uses stratified random sampling.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: The researcher first divides the defined membership population into relevant subgroups, or strata, based on session schedule. Invitations are then selected by chance within each subgroup. This provides a planned way to include both daytime and evening members rather than relying on who happens to attend when recruitment occurs.

The random element must operate within each group; simply inviting a convenient number from each schedule would instead be a quota-style procedure. The intended numbers and selection rule should be stated. Stratification concerns selection into the sample, not assigning a person to a treatment, and subsequent refusal can still affect the final coverage.

title: Sampling across two club schedules — Method comparison
stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** A fictitious class survey asks adult members of a community club about preferred ways of organising shared activities. With permission, a researcher obtains a current membership list divided into daytime and evening members. They randomly select invitations within each group. Selected members receive the same short questionnaire, but several say that the phrase “regular contact” is unclear. Participation is voluntary, and membership administrators cannot see individual answers.

Compare and contrast this stratified random approach with simple random sampling from the full club list.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Both use a defined membership list and chance-based selection rather than approaching only convenient attendees. Both still require informed consent, and both may be affected by a selected member declining the questionnaire. Neither sampling procedure makes a poorly worded item valid.

Simple random sampling selects directly from the full list, without first ensuring invitations to each schedule group. In a small sample, one schedule might receive few invitations by chance. Stratification deliberately structures selection across the two groups, which is useful when the research aim requires both schedules to be heard.

Stratification requires reliable group information and a justified allocation rule. Simple random sampling is easier when only the full list is available. The advantage therefore depends on whether schedule is relevant to the aim; adding strata mechanically does not guarantee that the final consenting sample represents every important difference between members.

stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** A fictitious anonymous survey asks consenting adult learners which forms of peer feedback they prefer. The form collects no names, contact details, identifying codes or device identifiers. The consent page nevertheless promises that an individual can have their particular answers removed up to one month later. Once submitted, the researcher cannot identify which response belongs to whom. The class wants to preserve privacy while making a realistic withdrawal statement.

Distinguish anonymity from confidentiality with reference to this survey.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Anonymity means that an individual response cannot be linked back to an identified participant through the retained information. The stipulated form collects no name or identifying code, so the researcher has no practical route to locate a particular person’s submission later. Confidential data are not automatically anonymous. The survey’s privacy strength does not make it possible to remove a particular anonymous response after it can no longer be identified.

steps.text: Test–retest reliability concerns the consistency of a measure across occasions when the underlying characteristic is sufficiently stable. Conversely, identical answers would not prove that the items measure the intended construct. The researcher must distinguish consistency from validity and consider the intervening circumstances.

stem:

Compare and contrast closed response options with open-ended items for this questionnaire.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Both ask participants to report their own experience of opportunities to interact, so both can be affected by memory, interpretation and willingness to disclose. Either can be administered privately at both occasions with voluntary consent; response format alone does not establish truthful reporting.

Closed options provide consistent categories and reduce the burden of answering, but may force varied experiences into an unsuitable choice. An open-ended item permits a participant to explain that scheduled groups increased some conversations while reducing others. The formats can complement one another if each serves the aim. A clearly defined closed item can establish a common reference period, while a neutral optional comment can reveal unanticipated meanings. stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** In a fictitious low-stakes classroom experiment, consenting adults are recruited through a volunteer notice. A chance procedure allocates them to two groups learning the same unfamiliar factual passage for the same time. One group sees a small-font, densely spaced version; the other sees a larger-font, widely spaced version. Both complete the same recall task. Distinguish random allocation from random sampling with reference to this experiment.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Random allocation assigns participants who have already joined a study to its conditions by a chance procedure. Here it concerns whether a consenting volunteer receives the small, densely spaced passage or the large, widely spaced passage. It can reduce systematic participant differences between the conditions, although chance imbalances remain possible in a small sample.

Random sampling concerns how people are selected from a defined population before participation. This sample was recruited through a volunteer notice, so chance allocation does not turn it into a random sample of all adults. Internal comparison between conditions and generalisation beyond volunteers therefore require separate consideration.

Compare and contrast this independent-groups design with a repeated-measures design using two equivalent passages.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Both can manipulate text presentation while using recall as an operational measure of learning. Both need consistent exposure time and equivalent instructions. The independent-groups design compares different people, whereas the repeated-measures design exposes the same participant to each condition.

Repeated measures reduces the influence of stable individual differences in memory because each participant contributes to both conditions. It introduces order and practice effects, and the passages may not be perfectly equivalent. Independent groups avoids direct carry-over between passages but may have uneven baseline memory ability, especially with few volunteers.

Counterbalancing passage and condition order can help a repeated-measures design, while random allocation and an adequate sample help independent groups. Neither choice solves the original two-feature confound. A defensible comparison therefore separates participant design from the need to isolate the intended independent variable.

stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** A fictitious class practical compares two harmless ways to learn unfamiliar words. Every consenting participant studies one list using spoken rehearsal and another using imagery. Half receive rehearsal first and half receive imagery first. Equivalent lists are rotated across the two orders. The teacher warns that participants may continue using imagery when later instructed to rehearse, so experiencing one strategy could alter the next condition. No findings are supplied.

Explain counterbalancing and what it can address in this procedure.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Counterbalancing varies the order of conditions across participants rather than giving everyone the same sequence. Here half receive rehearsal before imagery and half receive the reverse order, while lists are rotated. This reduces the risk that a simple first-versus-second position difference is always attached to one strategy.

It does not ensure that all order effects cancel. If learning imagery changes how someone later performs rehearsal, the carry-over may differ between sequences. Equivalent lists also require justification rather than merely being labelled equivalent. Counterbalancing is therefore a control for some order-related alternatives, not proof that the comparison is free of carry-over.

title: Practice that carries into the next condition — Method comparison
stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** A fictitious class practical compares two harmless ways to learn unfamiliar words. Every consenting participant studies one list using spoken rehearsal and another using imagery. Half receive rehearsal first and half receive imagery first. Equivalent lists are rotated across the two orders. The teacher warns that participants may continue using imagery when later instructed to rehearse, so experiencing one strategy could alter the next condition. No findings are supplied.

Compare and contrast repeated measures with independent groups for investigating these learning strategies.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: Both designs can compare the same strategy instructions using a common recall measure and equivalent material. Both require voluntary consent, standardised procedures and attention to the validity of what participants actually do. They differ in whether each participant experiences one or both strategies.

Repeated measures controls stable participant differences efficiently because each person contributes to both conditions. Here that advantage is threatened by strategy transfer: learning imagery may change later rehearsal. Independent groups removes that direct sequence within a person, but different memory ability or previous strategy experience can create between-group differences.

Chance allocation and an appropriate sample improve the independent-groups comparison. Counterbalancing and pilot checks improve repeated measures, although they cannot guarantee the removal of asymmetric carry-over. The preferable design depends on whether the strategies can be kept sufficiently distinct, rather than on a rule that repeated measures is always more controlled.

title: Confidence is not delayed recall — Method knowledge
stem:
**Constructed class-practical case.** In a fictitious experiment, consenting adults are randomly allocated to re-reading a short passage or trying to recall it from memory. Immediately afterwards, they rate how well they think they will remember it tomorrow. The researcher calls this rating a measure of next-day recall, although no next-day memory task is administered. All learning is low-stakes and ungraded, and volunteers can withdraw.

Explain why an operational definition must distinguish predicted memory from observed memory performance.

This self-contained item practises Paper 2A methodology. In an examination requiring your own class practical, use the practical you actually studied.

steps.text: An operational definition states how a construct is measured in the procedure. The rating measures a participant’s current judgement of expected future memory. It does not observe how much information that participant can actually recall after a day, because the stipulated procedure contains no delayed memory task.

Confidence and performance may be related, but the relationship cannot simply be assumed. A participant can feel fluent while re-reading without later reproducing the information accurately. The researcher should name the rating as a prediction or confidence measure and use an appropriate delayed task if the aim concerns next-day recall.

steps.text: Both approaches could collect confidence ratings after a learning activity, and both require a clear definition of the activity and outcome. title: A registered comparison of lunchtime walking routes
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious university team wants to investigate whether the setting of a short walk influences adults' immediate sense of restoration. Adults who regularly visit one public library volunteer after reading a notice. After private consent, a computer randomly allocates each volunteer to a quiet garden route or an indoor corridor route. Both walks last ten minutes and use recorded instructions with identical wording. Participants know which route they take. An assistant who does not know their allocation administers the same short self-report restoration questionnaire immediately afterwards. Before recruitment, the team publicly records its question, questionnaire and intended comparison. It also records reasons for any departures from that plan. Participants can stop walking or omit questions without losing their travel reimbursement. No diagnoses are requested and no treatment is offered. The researchers plan to describe their comparison as a test of how walking settings affect everyday restoration, and suggest that its findings could guide other public libraries.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: causality, measurement, bias, responsibility.

steps.text: Causality is strengthened by allocating routes randomly rather than allowing participants to choose a preferred setting. Standardising duration and instructions reduces alternative explanations involving time or different guidance. Nevertheless, the intervention is the whole garden-versus-corridor experience: noise, light and other features vary together. A difference would not isolate greenery as the single causal ingredient.

Measurement limits what any route effect means. The questionnaire measures reported immediate restoration, not a diagnosis, enduring well-being or physiological recovery. It should use clear items and evidence that their interpretation fits these participants. A later measure could investigate persistence, but cannot retrospectively turn the immediate self-report into evidence of a long-term improvement.

Bias remains possible because participants see their setting and may infer that the garden is expected to help. A masked assistant reduces one route for assessor influence but does not blind participants or make their reports objective. Neutral recruitment wording and questions about participants' expectations could clarify this threat without promising to eliminate it.

Recording the planned comparison before recruitment makes selective changes to the question or outcome more visible. Documented departures allow readers to distinguish planned decisions from later exploration. This is a transparency strength, not a guarantee of valid measurement or a representative sample. Library volunteers may differ from people who rarely visit libraries or cannot comfortably walk these routes.

Responsibility is supported by meaningful withdrawal, optional answers and reimbursement that is not conditional on completing the walk. Route accessibility and ordinary physical comfort still require attention. Overall, the design can support a bounded comparison of these routes for consenting library volunteers. General recommendations need replication in other libraries and attention to expectations and the meaning of restoration.

subject: psychology
title: Whose workday can enter a referral chain?
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** In a fictitious study, researchers want to understand how independent market traders describe opportunities to pause during their working day. There is no complete trader register. Recruitment starts with two stallholders known to a community liaison worker. Each consenting participant may pass a study leaflet to other traders, but does not give the researcher anyone else's contact details. Adults who respond choose a private interview time away from their stall. A researcher uses a common set of open questions and neutral follow-ups about ordinary pauses, without requesting medical information or income figures. Interviews are recorded only with separate permission. The researcher keeps a record of recruitment chains and of how their own assumptions influence follow-up questions. Recruitment stops when the agreed project period ends. The team intends to report different accounts of managing pauses, while a funder hopes the interviews will identify the priorities of all local market traders.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: bias, perspective, measurement, responsibility.

steps.text: Snowball recruitment is defensible when no complete sampling frame exists: the initial contacts provide access to traders who might otherwise be difficult to approach. However, referral chains follow social connections. Friends with similar schedules or established stalls may be repeatedly reached, while isolated traders and newcomers remain outside the invitation network. Access is therefore a strength without establishing population coverage.

Bias can enter before an interview begins. Starting from the liaison worker's contacts may privilege traders comfortable with community organisations. Recording chains makes this dependence visible but does not correct it automatically. Starting additional chains in different market locations and seeking less-connected traders would widen opportunities to participate; the resulting sample would still not become randomly selected.

Perspective matters because an interview elicits how traders understand a pause within their particular working relationships. The reflexive record helps readers examine why certain answers received follow-up questions. An alternative interviewer or discussion of assumptions could challenge the first interpretation. Neither agreement among researchers nor the label reflexive demonstrates that all relevant viewpoints have been captured.

Measurement concerns the distinction between accounts and observed routines. A trader may describe an ideal routine, a memorable busy day or a meaning of rest that differs from the interviewer's. Neutral clarification and concrete examples improve interpretability without treating inconsistency as dishonesty. Direct observation could add another perspective, but would raise different access and privacy issues.

Responsibility is strengthened by participants forwarding leaflets rather than disclosing other people's details, and by separate recording permission. Private scheduling can also reduce pressure from neighbouring traders. The funder's population claim exceeds this design. A defensible conclusion would describe the experiences represented in the recruited networks and the important voices still missing, rather than rank the priorities of every local trader.

subject: psychology
title: An identifiable success story in a small walking group
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious researcher proposes an intensive case study of one small community walking group after its meeting place becomes accessible by a new bus route. With permission, the researcher can examine the group's existing attendance records and meeting notes. Members may separately volunteer for interviews about changes in their experience of attending. Former members will also receive an invitation through an independent organiser. The researcher plans to compare records from before and after the bus route begins and to consider accounts that do not fit the organiser's description of a successful change. During the same period, meeting times and the group leader also changed. The area is small enough that a distinctive journey described in a report might identify a member even if their name is removed. The organiser suggests publishing the records online to make the evaluation transparent. The researcher wants to understand this group's changing opportunities for social activity, rather than diagnose members' well-being.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: responsibility, perspective, causality, change.

steps.text: The case study can connect attendance records, organisational decisions and members' accounts within one setting. Seeking former members and accounts that challenge the organiser's success narrative strengthens the range of perspectives considered. However, people who left may be harder to contact or less willing to return. Including their invitation is not evidence that their experiences are adequately represented.

Change is central, but a before-and-after sequence does not identify the bus route as its only cause. Meeting times and leadership changed at the same time. Members might also alter participation for personal reasons. A careful timeline and comparisons of competing explanations can improve the account while leaving the causal contribution of the bus route uncertain.

Records and interviews offer different perspectives rather than interchangeable measurements. Attendance establishes recorded presence, not the quality of social contact or a person's well-being. Interviews can illuminate what participation meant, but retrospective accounts may be shaped by the present situation. Convergence would support a particular interpretation; disagreement should be explored rather than discarded as a failed check.

Responsibility extends beyond removing names. Distinctive journeys or combinations of dates may allow neighbours to recognise individuals. The research team should seek appropriate permission for secondary use, minimise details and agree how quotations will be checked for disclosure risk. Organisational access to an archive is not automatically consent from everyone mentioned within it.

Publishing raw records would create a conflict between openness and participants' privacy. A documented procedure, carefully de-identified examples and an explanation of withheld material could support scrutiny without exposing the archive. Overall, this is a useful contextual explanation of one group's change. It cannot demonstrate a general well-being effect of bus routes, and credible reporting may require limiting detail despite the organiser's enthusiasm.

subject: psychology
title: Age groups learning an unfamiliar ticket machine
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious team studies how adults from two age groups approach an unfamiliar transport-ticket interface. Adults aged 18 to 25 and adults aged 60 to 70 volunteer through the same community centre. Everyone uses the same mock machine in a quiet room and receives the same explanation. The machine requires no payment or real journey booking. The researcher records the sequence of actions and asks participants to explain their choices after the task. Before starting, participants describe previous experience with touchscreens and public transport. The two groups developed in different periods and may also differ in education, transport habits or comfort with being observed. Participants can request larger text, take a break or stop. The researchers describe the study as a quasi-experiment because age-group membership is not randomly allocated. They propose that comparing the groups may explain how development changes a person's approach to unfamiliar technology.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: causality, change, measurement, perspective.

steps.text: Age is a naturally occurring grouping variable, so the researchers cannot allocate it as they would allocate an experimental condition. Standardising the task removes some situational differences, but does not make the groups equivalent in their earlier experiences. Calling the design a quasi-experiment accurately recognises a limitation; it does not itself establish age as the cause of different approaches.

The concept of change exposes the distinction between age differences and development within a person. A cross-sectional comparison cannot directly show how these individuals changed as they grew older. Cohort experiences with transport systems and education offer plausible alternatives. A longitudinal extension would address within-person change, although practice, attrition and historical changes would then also need consideration.

Measurement must distinguish the intended psychological approach from familiarity or interface accessibility. A slow action could reflect careful checking, unfamiliar vocabulary, reduced visual access or uncertainty about the task. Action sequences and participants' explanations provide complementary information, but neither justifies treating completion speed alone as a complete measure of learning or adaptability.

Different perspectives can prevent the younger group's preferred strategy being assumed to be the ideal standard. Asking participants to explain choices may identify sensible priorities such as avoiding an expensive mistake. Previous-experience information can clarify competing explanations, but collecting it does not guarantee that all relevant group differences can be removed or adequately measured.

Using a mock interface, providing breaks and allowing larger text make the task more accessible without putting travel or money at risk. Accommodations should be documented so their role in the comparison is clear. The strongest conclusion is about these volunteers' approaches in this setting. A general claim that ageing causes reduced technological ability would exceed the design and ignore plausible cohort and measurement explanations.

subject: psychology
title: Watching planning develop without counting the same skill twice
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious longitudinal observation study follows adults beginning their first term as community-event volunteers. With consent, a researcher observes each volunteer planning a small display at the start of the term and again near its end. Volunteers are told that the purpose is to understand planning approaches, not to assess their suitability for the organisation. On both occasions they arrange the same model materials to meet the same brief. An agreed coding guide records actions such as checking the brief, changing a plan and asking another person for clarification. Two observers independently code a selection of sessions after practising with the guide. They do not see the volunteer coordinator's evaluations. Some volunteers who become very busy may miss the second session. The coordinator suggests interpreting fewer requests for clarification at the second session as evidence of increased independence. Participation is optional and recordings are separated from the organisation's personnel records.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: change, measurement, bias, responsibility.

steps.text: Following the same people supports a discussion of within-person change rather than simply comparing unrelated groups. Nevertheless, the second session repeats both materials and brief. Familiarity with this task could reduce clarification requests without a general development of planning independence. Equivalent new tasks or further occasions could help separate specific practice from a broader change in approach.

Measurement is the main difficulty in the coordinator's interpretation. Asking a useful clarification question can be an effective independent strategy rather than dependence. Fewer requests might instead reflect confidence, remembered instructions or reluctance to seek help. The coding guide should distinguish the function and timing of requests and draw on several indicators, rather than make one count stand for the whole construct.

Independent coding and a shared guide make observations more systematic. Keeping coordinator evaluations hidden reduces one potential source of expectancy bias. However, observers can agree because the same narrow definition is consistently applied. Agreement would support consistency of coding, not demonstrate that the operational definition captures planning independence or all valuable forms of development.

Missing second sessions can bias the apparent pattern of change if the busiest or least comfortable volunteers are disproportionately absent. The team should document follow-up opportunities and reasons participants choose to provide, without pressuring them to return. It should compare the scope of its conclusion with who was actually followed, rather than assume the initial group is fully represented.

Responsibility requires a credible separation between research and judgements about a volunteer's role. Clear access restrictions, optional participation and recording arrangements support that separation; a coordinator's verbal reassurance alone may not. Overall, the study could describe changes in observable planning behaviour across a term. A stronger claim about developing independence needs broader measurement and a response to practice and selective follow-up.

subject: psychology
title: A randomly invited survey of a transition out of work
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious local research team wants to understand how adults describe the transition into retirement. An authorised community organisation uses its membership list to send study invitations to randomly selected adults who recently retired. Researchers do not receive the contact list. Those who consent complete a postal questionnaire at home, with a separate telephone-completion option. Several items ask whether respondents feel able to organise their own daily activities; an open question invites them to explain what a satisfying day now means. Researchers test the wording with a small group before the main survey and offer both completion formats consistently. Some invited adults do not respond. The organisation includes members who joined organised activities, but not all retired residents. A researcher proposes that this random invitation procedure represents the whole local retired population and that respondents' descriptions of their earlier working lives will show how their independence has changed.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: bias, measurement, perspective, change.

steps.text: Randomly choosing invitations gives listed members a chance-based route into the study and avoids an interviewer simply choosing convenient acquaintances. The sampling frame, however, consists of organisation members. People who have not joined organised activities are absent. The invitation procedure can therefore be random within that list while failing to cover the entire local retired population.

Non-response introduces a further possible bias after selection. Adults who find the transition especially easy, difficult or worth discussing might participate at different rates. Accessible formats can reduce some practical barriers, but do not prove that responders resemble all invitees. The team should report the recruitment and response process and qualify whose transition is being described.

Measurement of independence requires care because organising a day is not the same as doing everything without assistance. Some respondents may freely choose shared routines or support. Piloting items can uncover ambiguous language, while the open question allows meanings that the fixed items miss. Different survey modes may also shape disclosure or interpretation and should be considered when evaluating the accounts.

Perspective is valuable here: participants' definitions of a satisfying day can challenge a researcher's assumption that independence is always the preferred outcome. Yet an account of an earlier working life is reconstructed from the present. It is not equivalent to a measure taken before retirement. A prospective follow-up beginning before the transition would provide a different basis for examining change.

The organisation's role protects its contact list, provided participation choices are not disclosed back to staff without permission. The proposed population and developmental claims remain too strong. The survey could describe how responding members understand a transition and generate explanations worth following up. It cannot establish a representative trajectory of increasing or decreasing independence for every retired resident.

subject: psychology
title: Belonging and attendance without an assigned social activity
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious researcher investigates the relationship between participation in neighbourhood activities and adults' sense of belonging. Randomly selected members of several public-library mailing lists receive an invitation. Consenting adults complete a short belonging questionnaire and permit the researcher to ask how often they attended local activities during the previous month. No one is asked to join or avoid an activity. The questionnaire explains that there are no preferred answers and that library services will not be affected by participation. The researcher also asks about length of residence and availability of free time because these might be relevant to both activity attendance and belonging. The contact information is stored separately and deleted after participants have had an agreed opportunity to withdraw. A local newsletter editor wants to report that attending more activities creates a stronger sense of belonging. The researcher plans to explain what this correlational design could and could not justify.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: causality, measurement, bias, responsibility.

steps.text: The study is correlational because researchers measure existing attendance and belonging without assigning a social activity. An association could be consistent with attendance supporting belonging, but people who already feel they belong might attend more. Length of residence or free time could influence both. The design therefore cannot by itself choose the newsletter editor's proposed causal direction.

Measuring potential common influences makes the alternative explanations explicit. It does not establish that every important common cause has been measured accurately or included. A stronger conclusion would remain conditional on assumptions about those influences. A follow-up over time could clarify temporal order, but temporal order alone would still not remove all competing explanations.

Measurement should distinguish attendance frequency from the quality or meaning of social relationships. Many brief events may not create closer relationships, while one regular activity could be important. Recall over a month and a desire to appear socially involved can affect attendance reports. Clear definitions and neutral wording help, without converting retrospective self-report into an exact behavioural record.

Random invitations reduce convenience selection within the library lists, but the lists omit non-members and respondents still choose whether to participate. Socially connected residents may have more opportunities or motivation to respond. The researcher should distinguish the invited frame from the responding sample and avoid describing either as all neighbourhood residents without further evidence.

Responsibility includes making the lack of service consequences credible and separating identifiers from responses. Participants need a clear withdrawal deadline before linkage is irreversibly removed. Overall, the study can examine an association among participating adults and identify plausible interpretations. Public communication should preserve that uncertainty rather than turn an unassigned activity measure into advice guaranteed to improve belonging.

subject: psychology
title: Two accounts of a shared project, kept separately
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** In a fictitious interview study, adults who have recently worked together on a voluntary community project are invited in pairs to discuss what makes cooperation feel fair. Each person receives an independent invitation and consents privately. They are interviewed separately by a researcher who did not manage the project. Both receive the same opening questions and neutral prompts for examples of ordinary decisions. The researcher does not pass either account to the other person, and allows participants to decline discussion of identifiable third parties. Participants may check the accuracy of quotations proposed for the report, but cannot approve or reject someone else's interview. The team hopes that paired accounts will reveal different perspectives on a shared relationship. One researcher suggests that if the accounts disagree, comparing them will establish which participant has misremembered the project. The report will use changed contextual details where necessary to protect identities.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: perspective, responsibility, bias, measurement.

steps.text: Separate interviews provide room for participants to describe fairness without negotiating a shared account in front of their project partner. The common opening questions support comparability, while follow-ups can clarify different meanings. This is a strength when the aim concerns perspectives on cooperation. It does not make either account a complete objective record of the project.

The proposed treatment of disagreement is too narrow. Participants may notice different decisions, define fairness differently or occupy unequal roles, rather than one simply remembering incorrectly. Comparing accounts can illuminate those perspectives and the relationship between position and interpretation. Additional records might clarify particular events, but would not automatically determine whose overall experience of fairness is correct.

Measurement is therefore partly about what an account represents. A concrete example and clarification of a term can deepen understanding of fairness as experienced by that speaker. Counting matching statements, or assuming agreement proves accuracy, would miss the study's interpretive aim. Accurate quotation checking improves the representation of a participant's words without validating every interpretation made from them.

Bias could arise if the interviewer treats one partner as more reasonable or probes one account more sympathetically. Working outside the project-management relationship reduces one authority concern, but researcher expectations remain possible. A reflexive record and review of neutral probing can make such influences more visible. They should be considered alongside the particular conditions in which each account was produced.

Responsibility is especially important because confidentiality is relational: a partner could recognise a quotation even after names change. Independent consent, clear limits on sharing and attention to contextual details are appropriate safeguards. Pairing also must not pressure one adult to participate to preserve the relationship. Overall, the design can offer a nuanced account of different meanings of fairness, not a procedure for certifying one partner's story as the truth.

subject: psychology
title: Cooperation seen from one camera angle
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious observational study examines cooperation when consenting adult pairs build a model from ordinary craft materials. Researchers do not manipulate an independent variable. Pairs choose when to begin and can stop whenever they wish. A fixed camera records the workspace with separate recording permission, and a microphone records discussion. A coding guide describes observable events such as offering a tool, asking for a suggestion and altering a plan after a partner's comment. Two coders practise the guide before working independently on the recordings. The camera clearly shows the shared table but can miss a hand movement near the edge. One coder knows some participants from the community centre. Pairs vary in whether they have previously worked together. Researchers propose that a greater number of coded offers indicates a more cooperative relationship. They will invite participants to describe how the task felt, but will not use the study to judge anyone's actual relationship.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: measurement, perspective, bias, responsibility.

steps.text: A concrete coding guide makes the observational categories inspectable and helps different coders apply the same definitions. Recording permits an event to be checked again instead of relying on memory. However, events outside the camera's field can be missed. The measurement opportunity is therefore limited by the recording arrangement, not simply by how carefully a coder watches.

More offers do not necessarily mean a more cooperative relationship. A well-coordinated pair may need few explicit offers, whereas repeated offers might follow misunderstanding or rejection. Pairs also have different opportunities to use particular tools. The team should interpret events within their sequence and task context, rather than treat an isolated event total as a complete measure of relationship quality.

Perspective matters because the observers' visible categories and participants' experiences can differ. A participant might experience an unsolicited tool offer as supportive or controlling. Optional accounts could illuminate that meaning without replacing the observed record or functioning as an unquestionable final judgement. Differences between perspectives can be informative rather than evidence that one measure must be discarded.

Knowing participants can affect a coder's expectations, even with a shared guide. Where feasible, separate coders from prior relationships and avoid identifying information not needed for coding. Agreement between coders would indicate consistency on the recorded events, not demonstrate that their categories capture the whole construct. Recording itself may also influence how pairs present cooperation.

Responsibility includes consent to both participation and recording, clear access restrictions and an opportunity to stop without damaging community-centre relationships. The study appropriately avoids diagnosing real relationships. Overall, it can describe selected cooperative behaviours during a particular craft task. Claims about stable relationship cooperation require broader sampling of situations, careful measurement and attention to the participants' meanings.

subject: psychology
title: A transparent experiment with a deliberately narrow learning claim
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious research team recruits adult volunteers from one evening course to compare two ways of learning unfamiliar map symbols. A computer randomly allocates each participant either to generate examples of where a symbol could be used or to read matched examples supplied by the researchers. Both groups study the same symbols for the same time in the same room. Before recruitment, the researchers register the procedure, their primary learning measure and the rule for handling incomplete tasks. A later test includes unfamiliar routes that require applying the symbols, rather than repeating the study examples. A scorer uses an agreed guide without seeing group allocation. Participants are told that both learning approaches are being investigated and that the task does not affect course assessment. The team expects its study to inform how these particular symbols are taught. A course organiser instead wants the results to identify the best general learning method for all students.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: causality, measurement, bias, perspective.

steps.text: Random allocation supports a causal comparison because it makes group membership independent of deliberate researcher or participant selection. Matching symbols, time and setting reduces several alternative explanations. The two procedures still differ in the activity learners perform, so a difference would concern the complete generating-versus-reading comparison. It would not identify every mental process responsible for that difference.

The primary measure is application to unfamiliar routes. That aligns with a transfer question more closely than merely asking participants to repeat the original examples. However, performance can also depend on understanding route instructions or previous familiarity with symbolic maps. An agreed scoring guide and masked scorer reduce assessor influence while leaving the validity of the chosen learning measure open to evaluation.

Registering decisions before recruitment makes later selection of a favourable outcome or exclusion rule easier to detect. It does not prevent an ineffective manipulation, an unclear measure or departure from the intended task. The report should explain deviations and distinguish additional exploratory questions. Transparency improves the basis for scrutiny rather than guaranteeing a particular causal or educational conclusion.

Bias may still arise if participants consider generating examples the expected superior method and try harder. Describing both approaches neutrally helps but cannot fully conceal the activity being performed. A brief check on what learners actually did could assess adherence, provided it does not become a post hoc excuse to exclude inconvenient participants selectively.

The organiser's broad claim neglects perspective and scope: other learners, subject matter and educational aims may value different outcomes. Volunteers from one adult course studying map symbols do not represent all students or kinds of learning. Overall, the design can test a limited causal question well while justifiably making a narrow recommendation. Replication across settings and measures would be needed before proposing a universal best method.

subject: psychology
title: Device switching and learning in an evening language course
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious researcher asks whether adults' self-directed study routines are related to learning in an evening language course. Participation is independent of course enrolment and assessment. Consenting adults complete a short daily diary for two weeks, recording when they choose to switch between study materials and unrelated device activities. They do not provide messages, browsing histories or application screenshots. At the end, an independent assistant administers a low-stakes task involving language material introduced during the same period. No participant is assigned to switch activities or to maintain a particular routine. The researcher also asks about work commitments and prior language experience. Diaries are labelled with study codes, and participants can omit any entry. The researcher proposes that this minimally intrusive design can identify how routine switching and learning are related. A tutor suggests using any association to tell learners that switching devices necessarily reduces their learning.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: causality, measurement, bias, responsibility.

steps.text: The design measures naturally occurring routines, so it avoids requiring learners to adopt an unwanted study habit. It can investigate an association but cannot isolate a causal effect of device switching. Work pressures, previous experience or difficulty with the material could influence both switching and task performance. A learner might switch because the material is difficult, rather than switching being the original cause of that difficulty.

Recording potential common influences helps frame alternatives, but does not guarantee that those influences are completely measured or that other explanations disappear. The tutor's necessary causal statement is stronger still: an observed relationship does not establish the same effect for every learner. A controlled, ethical comparison could address a more specific causal question under different assumptions.

Measurement of switching depends on what participants notice, remember and decide to enter. The definition should distinguish moving between relevant learning resources from unrelated activity, since both involve a device change but may serve different purposes. Short daily entries reduce a long retrospective burden, yet the diary remains self-report rather than a complete digital trace.

The language task measures a particular form of learning over the study period, not every benefit of studying or the learner's general ability. Diary keeping may itself encourage participants to change routines or present them favourably. Independent administration separates the task from tutor expectations, but does not remove participant reactivity or differences in opportunities to study.

Responsibility is a strength of asking for limited routine descriptions rather than private communications. Separate participation from course assessment, protect code linkage and explain omission and withdrawal arrangements. Missing entries can also narrow what is known and should not be treated automatically as no switching. Overall, the design offers a proportionate description of routines and learning, while the tutor should avoid presenting it as a universal causal rule.

subject: psychology
title: A single learner whose archive contains only finished work
stem:
**Unseen research study: entirely constructed for practice.** A fictitious researcher conducts a case study of an adult learning to compose short pieces of music. The learner gives permission to examine a personal archive of dated finished compositions and teacher comments from the previous year. With separate consent, the researcher interviews the learner and former teacher about changes in planning and revision. The archive does not contain abandoned drafts, and the learner selected which pieces to preserve before the study was proposed. Near the end of the project, the researcher also observes one new composition session. The former teacher describes an important turning point, while the learner attributes development to several small adjustments over time. Both may review quotations concerning themselves but cannot edit the other's account. The researcher wants to explain how this learner's approach changed. A proposed public report includes distinctive compositions and comments that could identify the learner despite use of a pseudonym.

Discuss this study with reference to at least two of the following concepts: change, perspective, measurement, responsibility.

steps.text: The case study can connect dated products, teacher feedback, retrospective accounts and a new observation. These sources address different aspects of learning and can challenge a single simple story of change. Their variety is a strength, but does not make them independent or complete: the teacher comments concern the same selected products, and both interviews may be influenced by the preserved archive.

Measurement of changing strategy is limited by the absence of abandoned drafts and intermediate decisions. A finished piece can show what was produced, but not reliably reveal the planning route that produced it. The new session offers more direct access to process at one point in time. It cannot reconstruct the missing processes that preceded every earlier composition.

Perspective is particularly important when the teacher names a turning point and the learner describes gradual adjustments. These may reflect their different access to events or ideas about effective teaching, rather than a simple factual error. The researcher should evaluate the basis of each account and allow more than one scale of explanation, without automatically privileging the teacher's professional status.

Change also needs an appropriately bounded conclusion. Differences between finished works could involve changing task demands, feedback or selection of what was saved. The case can develop a plausible contextual explanation and identify evidence that would challenge it. Prospective collection of drafts and process accounts would strengthen future work, but cannot repair the historical archive by assumption.

Responsibility requires attention to recognisable creative work as well as names. Permission to inspect a composition privately does not automatically permit its public reproduction. Agree the use of quotations and extracts, consider copyright permission and reduce identifying details. Overall, this study can illuminate one learner's development through carefully compared sources. It cannot establish a universal sequence of learning or treat a selected success archive as the learner's entire experience.
